utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, Madam Registrar, and good afternoon, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Somebody must have run away with the idea that I am French speaking because each day I find number 5 switched on. I know it pleases you, Madam Fauveau. So all the accused are here. I notice that Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Stojanovic are absent. I suppose they are working on the case at their offices. Correct me if I'm wrong. It seems I am not wrong. Prosecution, I notice Mr. McCloskey, and that's just him. Dr. Haglund is present. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I know you're familiar with the Tribunal, so I welcome you back to the Tribunal. Could you kindly proceed with the solemn declaration and then we can move straight to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Haglund. You know what the procedure is. Mr. McCloskey will go first, and he will then follow -- be followed by various Defence teams on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Haglund. Could you first just tell us your -- your name and title for the record?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: William D. Haglund. I'm currently the forensic -- senior forensic consultant for the Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you hold a doctorate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's in physical anthropology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- and as I've -- as you know, I've explained to you, this will be an abbreviated direct examination because of the law in place now and because of your prior testimony. But I think we'll still spend a little time putting everything in context. Can you just give us a brief outline of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My bachelors is in biology, from University of California, Irvine. My Masters and Ph.D. are from the University of Washington, in Seattle, Washington. The degrees were both in physical anthropology with a focus on forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you do the same for your work experience?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My first forensic job was at the King County medical examiner's office in Seattle, Washington. An office that has jurisdiction over all sudden unexplained deaths, accidents, aside homicide, and natural deaths without medical attendance. We did from 17 to 1500 cases a year, with 100.000 autopsies. I was the chief medical investigator supervising 12 to 13 individuals who went to the scenes and did the investigations at scenes or in the case of homicides and other certain suspicious deaths working in cooperation with the police to do investigations. I also, for part times, supervised the autopsy staff, so I reviewed cases and I dealt with the media. And on cases that involved outdoor scenes that would involve skeletal remains or buried remains and I was the person who went to the scenes for those remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now your international work.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: International work. My first entree into the international environment was in 1992 or 1993 when I went to the United Nations Security Council commission for the -- on war crimes in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you briefly. I notice you are just look at some --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm just looking at my resume to remember where I was at certain years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've got your other reports from this case in front of you as well?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And then I will skip 1996 because that's what we're here for. 1997, for the High Commissioner for human rights, I did an assessment, some training, and exhumations in Somaliland, and again in 1999 I was with the commission of inquiry for East Timor and set the stage for forensic investigations there. In the year 2000 for the UN presence in Afghanistan as well as for the High Commissioner for human rights I did assessments and some exhumations in Afghanistan. For the years 2003 through 2004 and 2005 I did assessments in Iraqi Kurdistan, and Iraq and also worked with ICRC and the UN presence in determining how to set up a workable exhumation strategy for Iraq and identification of the victims in Iraq. From 1999 to the present I have an ongoing project in Cyprus identifying the dead from the 1974 conflict in Cyprus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's to your experience at ICTR, ICTY, back in the days when they were under one Prosecutor. Can he tell us what your first job was in ICTR. I don't want to give it short shrift but we need to go through it briefly, and we'll get to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My first trip to -- of several weeks it was Rwanda at the request of the international Tribunal for Rwanda and the request came through Physicians for Human Rights. I did an assessment to determine what it would take to do forensic work in Rwanda. I did assessments of graves and found out what the conditions of remains were around Rwanda, and determined the equipment, et cetera, what we would need to do forensic assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's not objection, but I don't know if it's something wrong with the transcript. Did he say what year that was in line 12? I don't know if they picked up or he didn't say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, during this assessment period, who were you employed by?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was -- I think I was paid by the United Nations. I went on behalf of Physicians for Human Rights but they didn't pay. I was paid by the United Nations, actually. As often you do when you go with the High Commissioner for human rights, you're paid by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well then keep explaining that outline, how that work --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- progressed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In January 1995 I was appointed the senior forensic consultant as an employee of the Tribunal in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what work did you do then as the senior person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I did -- brought in the teams. The teams through 1996 were provided by Physicians for Human Rights. I, as an employee of the United Nations, coordinated those teams and directed their work and determined the resources they had to work with, logistics, local arrangements, arrangements with the government, UN entities regarding security, et cetera, was responsible for reviewing previous forensic reports that had been done in Rwanda, responsible for writing the complete report at the end of the exhumations, was responsible for interacting with the media in regard to the forensic work. Reporting to and the advisor to the investigators at the Tribunal. That was among some of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you -- can you -- before that, can you just tell us a bit about PHR, what are they? We know about MSF, but what's PHR?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. The Physicians for Human Rights, it's a Boston-based NGO human rights organisation and they have a forensic history of doing human rights throughout the world, and shared a Nobel prize in 1997 for their work with the torture protocols and -- and land -- excuse me, for work on landmine issues, but they do other aids in Africa, other human rights work as well as forensics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And getting back briefly to your work at the ICTR, did you testify?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I testified twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what cases?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In the Kibuye Rwanda case, a grave of -- that involved 493 individuals. And in the Amgar garage case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get a bit into the Amgar garage case, which is known as the Prosecutor versus Georges Rutaganda, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The first case was versus Clement Kayishema.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how did that work in ICTR move towards the former Yugoslavia and when?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, my 1995 visit from Rwanda ended with a -- asking me to come to The Hague to look into forensics for the Yugoslav Tribunal. And following the first exhumation in February, late February of 1996, then I came to The Hague and I went with investigators to look at mass graves and to assess the conditions of the graves and how we might approach exhumations and examinations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which cases was that for?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Most of those in -- involved cases that were alleged to be linked with the Srebrenica massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So tell us your work for the ICTY, when it actually -- when the actual exhumation work began, and -- but -- and what your position was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the work began before -- just getting the equipment and all the stuff together and the logistics and arranging for staffing and who was going to come. The actual in-the-field work began July 7th, 1996, at the Cerska grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've I believe, described yourself as a forensic pathologist. Do you have any other specialties or experience in related fields?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: As I mentioned, and the medical examiner's officer I was totally familiar with the autopsy procedures with dealing with the media, with identification. I specialised in identification of unidentified remains and in dealing with families and death notifications, and -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about archaeology?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Most forensic anthropologists, there's -- the difference between archaeology and anthropology, in a -- across the world changes, it's difficult to pin down; in Latin American archaeologists are really anthropologist. In the United States we have two separate divisions. We have archaeologists, but many anthropologist do have some training and experience in forensic -- or anthropology -- archaeology as well as their specialty of forensic anthropology, and I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, aside from what you've described briefly as helping set up the logistics for the former Yugoslavia, can you tell us what your job was in relation to the exhumations and the -- the morgue work? What was your position there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I was the senior person as far as forensics at the Tribunal was concerned, and was responsible for setting up the morgue facilities, arranging for the logistics, the equipment and resourcing of the teams, dealing with NATO in the regards to their security. Dealing -- and I was the media representative for -- on the field. I dealt with the local communities and the government in regard to dealing with remains. And in the field at the actual exhumations, I directed those exhumations and then as -- as far as the autopsies were concerned, made sure that the staff was present enough to do the work, brought in the pathologists and the autopsy assistants and radiologists and evidence technicians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your work in the summer of 1996 for the Srebrenica case, where did you -- can you give us an idea of where you spent your time? I mean not in particular, but just the exhumation site, the morgue, other places?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My major -- my major place was at the exhumation sites, but I also had to deal with -- with the setting up the facilities, both in -- in Bosnia and in Croatia, as well at the end of the year dealing with the Ovcara exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us just a bit, you mention Croatia and Ovcara. Is the Ovcara exhumation related to the Vukovar case --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us your involvement in that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My first involvement was in the early 1990s when I went with the commission and inquiry in war crimes. And that continued and then in 1996 I began makes visits to the equipment we'd left behind earlier and -- in the past years, and then doing a local arrangements and how we would actually deal with the facility in Zagreb and the exhumations in -- in -- in Vukovar at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually oversee the exhumations in Ovcara or were you involved in it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in it. I had a senior forensic archaeologist who started the work and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was Dr. Douglas Scott. And then subsequently Melissa Connor did some of the -- did the ending archaeology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's get back to Bosnia. And you had mentioned you spent most of your time at the exhumation sites. Did you have people that had more experience in archaeology there helping you with those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely. We find that the south -- the Latin American -- the South Americans have much more experience than any Ph.D. anthropologist in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, now, most of the -- well, the reports and the record of testimony in detail is part of this record, so I don't want to go through that, but I do -- would like just for you to hit the high points, if you could, on a few of these graves. Let's start with the grave at -- at Pilica. Can you tell us just a bit about that, how big was it, how many bodies, but just in a very brief -- and I hate to say it, but we need to do -- somewhat cursory at this point.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a two and a half to three metre deep grave that ex ended by six by 28 metres. That's the grave space. It -- we ended up with 132 individuals, that's the minimal number of individuals, about 260-some individual units that we picked up, some of these are body parts, some of them were nearly complete individuals, some were complete individuals, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you found the most concentration of complete individuals?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were in one clustered assemblage at far end of the grave, at one end of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the deepest end of the grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's -- that's hard to say. It was the deepest end of the grave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to determine whether this grave had -- had been disturbed in some way?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not definitively, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I -- I wouldn't -- I wasn't going to be able to commit myself definitely if it had been disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Had -- and why -- why was that? If you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, our previous experience with the Lazete grave, which was absolutely obvious, and this grave it was not so -- so obvious. Much of the soil in the grave that -- the part that we had above the bodies was just like the soil outside of the rest of the -- of the surrounding area. The body parts, the minimal number was difficult to show that we had more parts that might -- than might be belong to the bodies that we had other parts for. They weren't commingled but they were scattered often throughout some of the fill. That's the soil above and around bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had no knowledge of any secondary graves or anything like that at this point in 1996, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have access to aerial image of September, October, those periods after the July period?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, we did. That was -- one of the ways we located the graves in 1996 was some initial aerial imagery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any aerial imagery of Pilica that indicated disturbance or no disturbance. Did you remember getting any aerial imagery on that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I saw one image taken after the August release to the media of -- of -- that said that -- portrayed trucks or machinery back at the grave at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you take any of that into account in your original report in your -- in your conclusions related to it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, let's -- let me ask you about Cerska. Again, briefly describe that, how many bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Cerska was a primary, undisturbed grave. There were 150 individuals in that grave; 147 of them died of gun-shot wounds. The 40 -- 40 some individuals that were randomly distributed amongst the other individuals had ligatures either associated with or hands wired behind their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Your conclusion that they died of gun-shot wounds, is that a conclusion you would make as -- in your position or is that something you are relying on from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I think one of the interesting parts of these exhumations is that for the most part they were not skeletal remains, they were fleshed remains for the most part. And the examination is done by the path -- the forensic pathologist and the anthropologist contributes to the ant -- pathologist's findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But whose job is it to determine cause of -- and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's a medical opinion because it goes on -- the death certificate was a quasi-legal document, and proof of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's -- briefly Nova Kasaba, the grave you dug there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba had four graves with respectively seven, 19, six, and one individual. They were shallow graves. 27 of the individuals had bindings around their arms behind their back. And the -- they all died of gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any indications where those victims died? Any of those victims or could you make any --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- conclusion at that point?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Definitely in Nova Kasaba grave number 2, the individuals had been killed in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were in kneeling positions with their torsos bent forward, their heads forward. Many of them were still in that position, some had fallen over sideways in that position. And the majority of those individuals, the -- had -- 95 per cent of them received gun-shots to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Lazete 2. Can you tell us a bit about Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Lazete 2 actually involved two separate assemblages of remains or graves. Lazete 2A was an undisturbed primarily grave that held 112 individuals. In the -- the number at hand, I would have to look it up, died of gun-shot wounds. Of the Lazete grave, 2B grave, was a primary disturbed grave that had 52 individuals in it. There was one other skeletal remains that we had recovered during the early assessments in April that we had also recovered, but that was a skeletal remains on the surface and not part of these graves. There were, I think, a total of 106 blindfolds with these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you finish the exhumation at Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, we concluded our exhumation, but we left -- the grave Lazete 2B, we had had torrential rains and the ground was becoming unstable that the and the grave was a deep grave of two and a half to three metres, and the walls began caving in. I knew that there was at least one individual in that grave, but I closed down the grave because of -- of security reasons, and that's in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me ask you a bit about the security. In -- you're doing this the summer of 1996. Just really a few months after the war had ended. Can you describe what the security situation was like, what sort of measures you were up against in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a tender post-conflict situation. NATO troops were negotiating to keep the peace, and major -- their major priorities were doing that. We, according to the date, the Dayton agreement, the NATO troops could, would, or may guard experts while they worked at the grave. The most we could get was periodic surveillance of graves before we had come to the -- been able to start working at the graves. We stayed on military bases, we had to travel in convoys with 50 calibre machine-guns and automatic weapons, soldiers guarding us at all times. Harrier jets flew over the sites while we were there. We didn't know if this arrangement with NATO would last because of their other priorities. We didn't know from one day to the other whether we could turn back to those graves, the next grave. That was a very tentative situation in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you under any pressure to get the work done and bring back evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was our goal for being there. So we had to maximise our time while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And on -- on that point I would like to ask you, from 1996 were there some complaints from some of your professional colleagues against you and against the chief pathologist, Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was -- did the UN take up a study and empanel an expert panel to review those complaints?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us the people on the panel, I'll briefly refer their names. Walter Birkby from Arizona; Vincent De Majo [phoen] from San Antonio, Texas; Richard Prouty [phoen] from Tucson, Arizona; Elis Curly [phoen] from California and Jerry Melby [phoen] From Mississauga, Ontario, Canada. Are these people of high esteem and reputation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly are. De Majo is probably the expert in the world in gun-shot wounds. I must say that in picking out this panel, they had a difficult time in not picking out a lot of people that I knew very well. So they tried to go for people that didn't know me, but they did pick out an excellent panel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, the -- let me go to the pathologist, Dr. Kirschner, who is now deceased. Was there a complaint that Dr. Kirschner had changed the cause of death on some of the autopsy reports without consulting the pathologists involved?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that confirmed by the panel, as to have happened?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did they find that to be improper?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They found that to be improper, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: However, they did find that the -- the Office of the Prosecutor had adequately went back and taken all of the reports back to the original pathologist to ensure that their findings and their final opinions reflected what their findings and final opinions were. And the -- this commission of inquiry then felt that they had adequately taken care of the problem. But still the issue with Dr. Kirschner, they thought was wrong, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the allegations against you, were they -- did -- were they upheld in any way?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were cleared?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to -- I want to go over just briefly some of those allegations. By my count there were 17 professionals interviewed by the panel. 13 of those were favourable to you, and four were critical. Let me start with the first criticism, and that is from Clyde Snow, who this Trial Chamber has heard a lot about. Can you tell us a bit about your knowledge of Clyde Snow, his reputation and your connection to him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I began working with Clyde Snow in the mid-1980s when we had a serial murder case in our jurisdiction, and I called on him to give us some consultation. And then subsequently did other forensic work with him. He actually was a mentor for me in many ways and he was very supportive at beginning of all the international work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is he one of the top people in this field?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, he certainly is the pioneer in international human rights forensic work and the application of forensic anthropology and archaeology, especially in the Latin American countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with him regarding the Ovcara grave in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, he invited me to be on that original inquiry in the early 1990s, and basically suggested I -- I -- I think had much to do with me being involved in the subsequent assessments of that grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he actually present when you were overseeing the exhumation of the grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Dr. Snow was consulting in regard to the ante-mortem database, which had been worked on by the Croatians for three years. And so he visited the grave of for a half a day at the time we were doing some of the cleaning of -- some of the original -- starting of the grave. I don't know if we had actually started removing remains at that time. But his -- his position as far as human rights was concerned, to give me information and we talk about the identifications and it was up to me whether I accepted them or not, and then what we would do with those identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me read to you the panel's synopsis of -- of Dr. Snow's comments about you, and I believe he's referring to the Ovcara grave. "Clyde Snow, Ph.D., states 'obviously sloppy work was done. He felt at times it was Dr. Haglund versus the UNTAES and mentioned the many bodies removed on one day. Dr. Snow stated in his opinion no more than 20 bodies have you had have been exhumed in a single day. He felt Dr. Haglund showed very poor judgement and it was lucky nothing had blown up as a result of the procedures used."' First, can you tell us what UNTAES was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: UNTAES, that was the transitional UN authority that was present in eastern Slovenia at the time. And they provided wonderful logistics to us while we were there, and actually enabled us by the tent they put over -- warehouse tent they put over to complete the grave in bad rain season.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you respond to Dr. Snow's criticism that you were removing bodies too fast and that no more than 20 bodies should be removed at any day?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I've never seen a proclamation like that before; it's certainly not in the literature. And these were fleshed remains. I have to say that the -- the rate at which you can remove bodies or human remains, skeletal remains or bodies from a grave is dependent upon many factors. First of all, it's is the condition of the remains. It makes a big difference if you're dealing with fresh remains and you pick them up in one piece. But when you're picking them up as skeletons you're picking them up in about 150 pieces. That makes a difference. It makes a difference how the bodies are distributed. Are they in one pile? Are they distributed over a large area? With partially skeletonised remains, like the Surstika [phoen] grave, was convenient because they were -- they were over an area stretching on for 30 metres. And you could deploy many people in exhuming many parts of the grave. Once you take a grave like Lazete 2A, once you have removed the dirt from around these graves, these bodies, they are just bodies that are stacked against each other, and it's just a matter of peeling them away from each other. The limiting factor is the documentation of the remains in the grave before you do that. And it's photography and the mapping, and if you have very good mappers, you can do that very fast, probably in less than five minutes a mapper could outline the bodies in a grave. So it depends on how you can deploy your staff, the number of staff you have, the condition of the bodies, the circumstances of the grave. To make the point of how many -- how -- how the bodies are deployed, if the bodies are all in one -- one latrine or in one well, then you can only get one worker down there at a time. But if you can get 10 workers out in a grave at a time, it makes a difference how much work you can get done in a day. I look at this from the assessment point I have to look at how long it might take to dig a grave, I look at the average amount of remains that are removed from the time you start because it depends upon when the bodies are cleaned and exposed that you can remove them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if the criticism from Dr. Snow is based on his own personal observation of you removing bodies or that of others?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, he was only at the grave at one time. Half a day or just for a visit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next criticism is from Dorothy Gallagher, an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And she says, "Saw problems in the field and in the lab stated Dr. Kirschner changed autopsy reports and instructed her to do so while processing the reports. In the field Dr. Haglund directed --" excuse me "-- dictated too much speed in exhumation. The result was commingling and failure to associate body parts." I think you've -- now this is -- Gallagher is from the Bosnia exhumations, Dr. Snow was from the Croatia Ovcara exhumations.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we again see the same criticism. Do you have anything to add to the speed criticism or response?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I -- when you're working with so many people from so many different backgrounds, anthropologists, archaeologists, especially from other countries, are not accustomed to working in a medical-legal system with a forensic pathologist at all and they're not accustomed to working in an office where you have a certain -- you have an uncertain workload every day and you have to be efficient and you have to get on with business. And -- and I think that was part of a perceptional thing and I can understand, because when you -- you have days or so to do work or months to do work, that's one thing. This was not the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did commingling result as -- because of the way you removed these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Commingling results from one of three major sources, either bodies are commingled when they're put in the grave, bodies -- skeletons -- as bodies skeletonise, remains are especially stacked one on top another, they can become commingling through the natural processes of the decomposition, or they can become commingled as they are removed from the grave. In the Cerska grave -- I think in Nova Kasaba there was no commingling, there was basically none in the Pilica grave, Lazete grave, I -- there may -- I'm not sure. There were 12 incidences of commingling in -- in the Cerska grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did this happen as a result of you exhuming bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, and what we did to try -- the best place at times -- you do good documentation where you get remains from, the best place to resolve some of these commingling problems is in the laboratory where you can clean the bones and you can look at them. And what we did is, made sure that we knew exactly what areas and what bodies were in association with these remains and then we had the pathologist who did the bodies from that group, those same pathologists do all the bodies from that group so there would be a historical memory, what was missing and what was there. And that helped on -- with the commingling problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go on to the last of that group. David del Pino, a Chilean anthropologist, he notes that, "Operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. Clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identification."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That, "clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though it contained identification," is that true?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, part of this would be true. Yes. The clothing issue. On associated clothing in graves of -- in the Cerska grave we had unassociated clothing. We took them back to the lab, they had no connection to any bodies, and if they have no documentation in them, then when you turn the bodies over to the Bosnians, they don't even want it. What do you do with it? That was our first experience with it. By the time we got to the Pilica grave, and this is the grave that I think Mr. del Pino is referring to, we had some unassociated clothing. As I mentioned in the Pilica report at page 20, I had to search for documents, there were none, and it was my decision to leave those unassociated clothing in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Rest of those comments were more to do with management. It says forms were not always used. And there was no delegation of authority. I might as well say it all. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, delegation of authority, when I -- when I was not present, the other UN expert at the site would be Jose Pablo Baraybar, who I think has testified in this trial. He was in charge when I was gone. I think the perception that I slow down the process is that while I was gone I learned from the first grave that it was necessary for one person to have -- be the conduit between the laboratory facility and the exhumations and the grave, and that person was me because I was able to travel back and forth but these other people weren't. So I insisted that before remains were removed that I be there and that I transcribe a short description of the bodies so they could be matched with the clothing and the description of the body once they got back in the grave and that is what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: But it did not slow down the work. I guarantee you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to read to you the brief finding of the report relating to you and get your reaction, if any, to it. Under the list of findings, it says, "The responses of the witnesses did not indicate any actual wrongdoing on the part of Dr. Haglund, nor anything regarding the exhumations that jeopardised their scientific validity. The pathologists who were working in the morgue made no complaints about the exhumation of the bodies or the conduct of the anthropologists who were working in the morgue or at the grave sites. Rather, it became apparent that the main problem with the exhumations were administrative and logistic; whether real or imagined, there were concerns regarding international politics imposing a great deal of pressure on the teams to complete the exhumations quite rapidly. Even so, there was little or no evidence that the pace of the examinations adversely affected the overall scientific quality. Along with the pathologists the most experienced archaeologist stated the recovery of bodies had been done adequately under difficult circumstances." Do you have any disagreement with those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I agree with it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One last matter before turn you over to -- for cross-examination, and that's a serious matter that I think you informed us about a few weeks ago, I believe now, that something you had just learned. And that is a judgement in a Rwanda case that basically set aside your scientific method, and that would be the case of the Prosecutor versus Georges Rutaganda, case number ICTR 96-3-T, that judgement was in the 6th of December, 1999. And that judgement was affirmed by the Court of Appeals on 26 May, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't intend to retry a Rwanda case, but I think, Your Honours, and if I could ask the witness a few questions about this, I think it would -- may save time. And if I could start by -- there's a short section in the indictment in that case which lays out the factual basis by which his testimony was predicated and I think is a very useful way to make sense out of the criticisms and the Court's brief judgement on the point. So I will quote from the section of the indictment that's applicable to the exhumation. "In April 1994 on a date unknown, Tutsis, who had been separated at a roadblock in front of the Amgar garage, were taken to Georges Rutaganda and questioned by him. He thereafter directed that these Tutsis be detained with others at a nearby building. Later Georges Rutaganda directed men under his control to take 10 Tutsi detainees to a deep, open hole near the Amgar garage. On Georges Rutaganda's orders, his men killed the 10 Tutsis with machetes and threw their bodies into the hole." Now, I want to go to page -- or paragraph 256 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. "The Chamber notes furthermore that Witness Q identified the hole where the 10 persons were killed and where their bodies were thrown on the slide tendered by the Prosecutor as Exhibit 168. The Chamber observes that the said slide shows the site identified as RUG 1 by Professor William Haglund, a forensic anthropologist, who appeared as an expert witness for the Prosecution. According to Professor Haglund, who exhumed several sites near Amgar garage, three bodies were exhumed from the hole identified as site RUG 1. Dr. Nizam Peerwani, a pathologist who had worked jointly with Professor Haglund and who had also appeared as an expert witness for the Prosecutor, submitted the following findings on the three exhumed bodies. The first body was that of a managed between 35 and 45 at the time of death, the probable cause of which was homicide. "The second body was that of a woman aged between 30 and 39 at the time of death, the probable cause of which was homicide. "And the third body was that of a managed between 35 and 45 at the time of death, the probable cause of which was blunt force trauma." Now, the next paragraph, paragraph 257 comments: "Firstly, the Chamber, on the basis of the testimony by Dr. Kathleen Reich, a forensic pathologist called by the Defence as an expert witness, is not satisfied that the scientific method used by Professor Haglund is such as to allow the Chamber to rely on his findings in the determination of the case." Next paragraph: "Secondly, and above all, the Chamber notes that the Prosecutor failed to show a direct link between the findings of Professor Haglund and Dr. Peerwani and the specific allegations in the indictment. Consequently, the Chamber holds that the findings of said expert witnesses should not be admitted in the incident case." All right. So paragraph 258 is the Prosecutor didn't meet their burden. But paragraph 257 says they are not satisfied with the scientific method used by you. Now, I want to go to the paragraph preceding that, where they're talking about things that include scientific method and see if we can identify who did what. Now, the first part that I see as a potential scientific method would be the first body was that of a managed between 35 and 45 at the time of death. Was determining the age range at the time of death your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was a contribution of the anthropologist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that -- was your scientific method involved in that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "The probable cause of which was homicide." Did you make that determination yourself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, that's a determination made by a -- a medical doctor, Dr. Peerwani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that in part based upon your -- your findings or assistance in the review of the bones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to the next one. "The second body, woman aged between 30 and 39." Again, that age determination was your scientific method, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the probable cause was homicide. So that is Dr. Peerwani's?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The third body was that of a man aged between 35 and 45 at the time of death. That again is your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Probable cause was blunt force trauma, that's Dr. Peerwani's?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there is no other mention that I could find about what particular scientific method the -- of yours the Court set aside, but in re -- have you had a chance to review the testimony of Kathleen Reich now?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find her criticising your method used to put an age range for the remains?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. Can we know which method she criticised then or what she criticised to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I think the question indicated, they were -- there was -- Dr. Haglund nor myself have been able to find any criticism of the -- in the -- in her testimony or the report of his method of aging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did she criticise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are on our way, and I -- it's not -- it's not clear in the judgement, but we do -- I will ask him some questions where that should become clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, that's my next question. What scientific method did she criticise, and I -- let me ask you the -- about the -- the -- there was a lot of time spent on cross-examination about -- in fact, let me go right to a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe in this Tribunal y'all can take judicial notice of a trial judgement, an appeal judgement from the ICTR. Now, Mr. McCloskey says he doesn't want to retry the whole Rwanda case but apparently that's what he's going do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He won't get a chance to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He won't get a chance to do that. Neither he nor the witness. But if the judgement refers to the testimony of this person as criticising the methodology of -- supposedly because it's not even clear whether it's just his or also the other experts. And he has said that in her testimony she doesn't criticise his methodology in trying to reach the age of -- of the persons exhumed, then in order to be able to understand what we're talking about, we need to know whether she at least criticised anything. I mean, not bringing into question the -- the judgement either of the Trial Chamber or of the Appeals Chamber. I mean, far from it, I wouldn't dream of doing that or allowing anyone to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will briefly outline those to give you a picture so that this makes more sense as we continue into cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go to -- it's page 38 of the testimony of expert Reich and there is a question by Defence counsel, it says, "Right. And do you recall, if in Dr. Haglund's report there was a conclusion as to cause of death for this site? "A. Well, I had difficulty with this as well. He concluded, I believe, that the cause of death, the manner of death was homicide. And that was based on trauma patterns in the skull and the fact that I believe there were nine individuals represented but only five skulls. The manner of death is homicide, was based on the fact that there was trauma in those skulls, that and the ages of the individuals was young." Now, just to reiterate, in your report did -- were the conclusions as to cause and manner of the death your conclusions or those conclusions of Dr. Peerwani?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: As inflected -- reflected in his autopsy reports, they are his conclusions. I only summarised those for the overview of the report. And I might say she's only referring to a -- a group of -- of bones, I think, referred to as RUG 4. There were nine minimal number of nine individuals of bones that were -- had been picked up by locals and put in a pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And to -- just -- this won't take too long, to just get this in further context so you see the picture, and -- one more issue of criticism: "And do you recall from looking over Dr. Haglund's report what age estimates were actually given to those remains?? "A. I would have to go back to that, but I believe that there were some at least as old as 45 or so up into their 40s. The other problem is he states in the report that information regarding the specific -- the collection of these bones and their original resting place was completely lacking. This was a surface collection, there was no information whatsoever about where these bones had come from, where they had originally been, if they had buried or if they had not been buried. And he also concluded they were consistent with individuals who had died in 1994 without knowing their original context into what they had been subjected. It's impossible to make a statement like that." I want to direction your attention now to: Did you, in fact, say that in reviewing these bones that it was consistent with individuals that you had reviewed in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you conclude, based on that consistency, that that was a firm date for their date of their death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No it's consistent, it could be at other times, you just could not rule it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you agree with her statement that it's impossible to make a statement like "consistent with"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, we do that quite frequently. But I -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to turn this into --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- an argument, but -- so. But if you want to explain anything, feel free.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us briefly what other criticisms she made of you and respond to that, briefly?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. There was a criticism that -- that insect information was not used to determine a closer approximation of the time of death. There was a criticism that analysis of fabric and clothing was not used as an indication of time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were both those things true? Did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Those are not routine analyses that are done in Canada or the United States, and I could go into it further, if you wished. But they're not applicable. If they even were routine, they were not applicable to Rwanda, there are no standards for estimating, using insects to estimate time of death in Rwanda, there are no standards anywhere yet in the world for estimating time of death from fabric. Another one was the not taking skull -- casts of the skulls. That is not a new -- a routine thing that we would do in the United States or Canada. The usefulness of that would be to put clay on the skull and try to see if somebody recognised it as an individual and that's an impossibility in a population where there are 800.000 missing and dead individuals. I believe also the stature, it mentions stature. We used formulas that are population based to estimate stature. There are no standards for stature, so it really wouldn't matter what stature estimate that one would use because you couldn't even confirm it. There's no documentation of stature either in the former Yugoslavia cases that we worked on, nor in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did -- were you asked to comment on her testimony after it occurred or any evidence put on in the rebuttal case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did do a recross. Not after her testimony, no. I don't believe -- maybe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I did in regards to the report. I did answer questions addressed in this report in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Who's going first from the Defence teams? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I apologise for taking so much time to get set up here, but I wanted to get this extension for my microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haglund, how are you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's not working. Okay. There it is. Very briefly, we have about 15 minutes before the break. If I can just ask you a few quick questions on your direct, extensive direct testimony today being a 94 witness and not a live witness. From what I take it, all of the people, and we'll get into this a little more detail later, all the people who made allegations against you in San Antonio in 1997 were wrong?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which ones were right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I think there's mis -- misperceptions on the part of, for instance, the clothing issue, but I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, I'll ask you the question. During your direct testimony you more or less indicated that the individuals who had made allegations against your sloppy work, your ineffectiveness in the field, your being in front of the cameras all the time, your slowing up the process, I think you have indicated to the Prosecutor that those allegations were not true. Now, did I misunderstand your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't think I portrayed my response to Dr. Snow's criticism of the 20 bodies. I just explained what -- what the variables are in removing bodies. And it's grave-dependent. Maybe he's thinking of another grave, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How about -- we'll get back to Dr. Snow later. How about Dr. Gallagher's accusations. You're saying she's wrong, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's not Dr. Gallagher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How about Gallagher's accusations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was her perception; it was not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So again those accusations were incorrect or wrong?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And how about del Pino, Dr. del Pino?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He's not a doctor either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He's a an archaeologist, isn't he, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah. And where's he from, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He's from Chile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And didn't you testify on direct that the South Americans archaeologists are much, much higher skilled in this field than the American archaeologists, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you saying that del Pino, the allegations and accusations he made in San Antonio were also false?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: What does his exhumation expertise have to do with discarding clothing with -- and he did not know that we searched it for documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And then we go -- are those the only three he asked you about? Do you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Quizzing the witness on how many people I asked him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't have the luxury of having -- I will just disregard that, Judge. I will strike the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: In the Krstic testimony which you gave, I believe, May 29th, 2000 in this very building; is that correct? Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, it's been indicated to this Trial Chamber that this was new information, serious, a very serious matter and new information which you brought to the attention of Mr. McCloskey or the OTP here.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Could you be more specific about the information. I don't know what you are addressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Hang on. I'll certainly do that. If you can go to page 23, line 12.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's the wrong testimony. And that would be in book number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Hang on, not in your file, sir. Let me just tell you, Mr. McCloskey asked you a question on line 13, page 23 today, he says, "All right. One last matter before I turn you over to -- for cross-examination. And that's a serious matter that I think you informed us about a few weeks ago, I believe. Now, that has something you had just learned and that is a judgement in a Rwanda case that basically sets aside your scientific findings or method." Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the question, but if you say I did, I did. This has slipped my mind. This isn't the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, this was a few minutes ago --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm getting confused of what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the prelude by -- from Mr. McCloskey before he asked you questions on your Rwanda decision or judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, I'm talking about your testimony today. Did you, in fact, just learn of this judgement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I learned it -- of -- in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: February of this year?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Excuse me, January of this year, to my knowledge. That's my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How did you learn about it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was passed to me by an e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who sent you the e-mail, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who sent you the e-mail, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. It was a -- another anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And could you please state the name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Stefan Schmidt [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And according to the record, this judgement was actually entered the 6th of December, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well before you testified in the Krstic trial, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you were proofed, prior to your testimony in Krstic, who did the proofing? Was it Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did he and you -- did you and he discuss the Rwanda judgement then?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever learn of the Appeals Chamber judgement in that Rwanda case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what I think we're talking about now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm still talking about the Trial Chamber judgement that found your scientific unreliable and basically wouldn't accept your evidence. That was in 1999. December 6th.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. That was not -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Wasn't brought to my attention. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you said you found out about it a few weeks ago by an e-mail?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My question is when, if at all did you learn about the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Rwanda case which upheld the Trial Chamber's finding that your methodology didn't float or wouldn't fly?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's when I found out about it; this year. I found out about it this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to your Krstic testimony, I want to ask you first, you were very well aware on May 29th of 2000 of the San Antonio investigation, were you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, you were there and you testified, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I believe you answered to a question that the Prosecutor put to you that this was a United Nations -- the United Nations had put this together, this oversight committee, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the Office of the Prosecutor did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor did, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that's part of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And did they pay for this? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall being asked at page 3716 on May 29th of 2000 in the Krstic case, question by Mr. McCloskey, and -- "also at the end of this very long summer did one or two of your young colleagues have some criticism regarding your supervision of the archaeological work." Your answer was, "Absolutely, yes." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. "What was that about?", he asked next. Your answer, "Well, there was some criticism raised regarding the procedure, rate and quality of the work. Basically that was the crux of it." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the very next page, 3761, you're asked by Mr. McCloskey in Krstic, a question on line 10: "Q. And more significantly, were there -- well, did anyone -- were there any complaints regarding your work at the morgue and your anthropology work?" Your answer: "Not that I'm aware of, but there was a complaint raised regarding the supervising pathologist and the autopsy report." Do you recall that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony today that no one raised any complaints regarding your work, your anthropology work? Prior to your testimony in Krstic, and I'm specifically talking about what led up to this San Antonio oversight committee and people who testified there and gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The statement was "your anthropology work at the morgue," I believe, was the statement that he's quoting and now he's gone to anthropology work, which could lead --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Question, page 3761, by Mr. McCloskey to you in the Krstic case, May 29th, 2000: "And more significantly, were there -- well, did anyone -- were there any complaints regarding your work at the morgue and your anthropology work?"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, that question wasn't "your anthropology work at the morgue," was it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- that's what I took it to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's what you took it to mean?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you knew, didn't you, and you answered, not that you were aware of, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: At the morgue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But, seriously, you knew, you knew, did you not, that there were other complaints about your work as an anthropology -- or your anthropology work, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was answering it in context of this commission's report and the complaints that I was addressing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, to go back again, you've already testified in Krstic under oath that only one or two young colleagues made criticisms regarding your supervision of the archaeological -- archaeology work, didn't you, sir, under oath?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you know, you've seen this report on the oversight committee and you've read it --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would like to put on e-court, if possible, D270 [sic], which is the report of the oversight committee, and specifically, for e-court purposes, I would like to show page 0004 to 0005. If we could have them side by side. All right. Let's just scroll up a little bit. Down -- that way. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral VI, the comments by colleagues, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Number V, Clyde Snow. Are you saying Clyde Snow was not making any comments regarding your activities in 1996 in the Srebrenica area and only in the Croatian -- at the Croatian site, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what this was in reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it could mean sloppy science. Maybe that is a criticism of me any my anthropology. It's a sloppy science. It's very general. You could construe that as being that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I am getting the feeling that you could construe things a lot of ways. But anyway, I want to ask you, sir. My question was just this: Is it your understanding or testimony that Clyde Snow's observations or comments only went to your actions or activities or work at the Croatian site?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was the only place he was, at the morgue in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. We have to go to the next page, real quick. You see number 11, Patrick Myers, archaeologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He thought your behaviour was reprehensible?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He also stated your integrity at the site was compromised by your own self-promotion. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And of course you deny that, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't deny his perception of it. In his mind, yes, it was. Those are his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you're saying it wasn't true, it was just his perception, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: How am I supposed to say that I -- how can I evaluate -- let's see, how can I evaluate my reprehensible behaviour. You're asking me to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, was it reprehensible?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then you're saying he's wrong.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: People can have different perceptions. They can be right ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me ask you this question: How about Gallagher, Dorothy Gallagher?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: She thought you dictated too much speed, causing commingling, failure to associate body parts, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: David del Pino, number 14, a Chilean anthropologist, he said that you halted operations while you were away; clothing was discarded at your command even though some contained identification; forms were not always used; there was no delegation of authority. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These issues are all covered in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, they weren't covered in your testimony in Krstic, were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe many of these were addressed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, they were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: John Gerns, the administrator, found you to be aggressive and have a condescending attitude which had an adverse effect on the mission. And again, that was his perception, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's personality, not science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to your testimony in Krstic, are all those people I just named, Clyde Snow, Patrick Meyers, Dorothy Gallagher, David del Pino, John Gerns, were they -- were they the one or two young colleagues that had some criticism of your supervision at the site when you said yes to that question in the Krstic case, page 370 -- 3760?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They are certainly the ones that are portrayed in the -- in the oversight committee's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that there were a lot more colleagues than one or two young colleagues who criticised your supervision of the archaeological work of the Srebrenica area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that's always to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Then why did you -- can you tell the Trial Chamber - and they have access to this record; it's in evidence - can you tell them why you didn't explain, Well, wait a minute, there were a lot more criticisms about me? Why did you hold that back, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That assumes a fact that's not in evidence. We can argue all day who are his colleagues, who was at the site. John Gerns is not his colleague. Dr. Snow was not at the site. I think that makes three and not two. We can argue over that all day long, but that was the question by the Prosecutor, whoever he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure that if we have a break now, Mr. Meek will rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, and especially to the court reporter and to the interpreters, I apologise. I will try to not speak so fast, and my colleague, Mr. Lazarevic, has promised to hit me if I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Promises are short-lived, Mr. Meek. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe you're right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, we do speak the same language, so -- do you have a transcript on either one of those screens?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, here there is part of the transcript from the committee oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What I'm talking about a LiveNote, do you have --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. The transcription? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What I'm going to try to do is wait until the cursor stops before I ask you another question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if you would try to do the same thing, maybe we'll make the lives of the court reporters and the interpreters and maybe everybody else a little bit easier. Okay. I know you're not a lawyer, and therefore I'm going to go back to your testimony in the Krstic case which was May 29th of 2000. Now, you do recall testifying in this building in that case, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, before you testified you were proofed, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Proofed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, did you have a session with a prosecuting attorney to go over what your testimony would be? That's what we call proofing.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you had a proofing session before your testimony in this case today also, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's true that the prosecuting attorney for the OTP was Mr. Peter McCloskey in both those cases, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is it your testimony then that when he asked you Krstic at page 3760 that at the end of that very long summer did one or two young colleagues have some criticism regarding your supervision of the archaeological sub-work, you said, "Absolutely, yes."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.
