Is it your testimony today that had Mr. McCloskey asked you, well -- a question to the effect of, Well, wasn't it more than just one or two colleagues, didn't, in fact, some very senior people in the field have some criticisms about your work, that you would have then answered "yes"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I said one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And which one was that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Clyde Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And so you don't -- you don't believe then that Patrick Meyers, an archaeologist, I mean was he a young colleague?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He was a -- a -- yeah, he was a young colleague, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He was actually doing our mapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What do you mean by young, age wise or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is gone over. It is more to do with the Prosecutor's question than it is the witness's answers too. So its relevancy is slim to none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's not. I'm just going about this a different way, and I'm trying to rephrase the questions because obviously, in my opinion, a lot more than one or two young colleagues that made criticisms about his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but let's try to be specific rather than going -- your cross-examination, you've got much more licence than the other side on direct. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: David del Pino, the archaeologist from Chile, do you also consider him to be a young colleague?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: At my age, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. When you say at your age, and trust me, I won't ask you that, was everybody mentioned in this report, besides Clyde Snow, younger than you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I really -- I really don't know, some of them were probably the same age. I can't answer that question, I don't know. I don't know everybody's ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also in that report -- and by the way, you were interviewed, were you not, along with Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe he -- he also appeared before this committee also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber -- well, wouldn't Peter McCloskey, a prosecuting attorney from the OTP, and Jan Kruszewski also present in San Antonio?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you in your job, you were the senior person, forensic pathologist on those exhumations, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was the senior forensic consultant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you were in charge of all the people working, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. There were some findings by that panel in San Antonio, were there not, that dealt with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And one of them, they state, and again I'm going to ask to have put up on the e-court, which would be page 007 of 2D70. And Mr. Haglund, just tell me when you see that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You were in charge of administration and logistics; you already testified to that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in the findings there you see that about halfway down in the fourth, fifth line, it says, "Rather it became apparent that the main problems with the exhumations were administrative and logistic." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: They also say under paragraph 1 on that page, do you see it? On the screen.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It says, "There were no systematic briefings at the sites upon arrival. No one seems to have been given any standard plan of operation. There was apparent disagreement as to the primary purpose of the mission." And it finishes with, "There was no clear concept of the chain of responsibility." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with what some thought, but of -- of -- in part, yes, that's -- that's certainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well -- and Mr. Haglund, I'm not agreeing -- I'm not asking you to agree with what some thought, because I'm asking you to agree with the findings of this committee that was paid for and put together by the OTP. And do you agree with those findings under paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If that was their findings, yes. Yes, if -- if they -- if they interviewed these people and that was their findings, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with the findings --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- Contained in paragraph 1, and not just because they found it, I'm asking you personally, sir, do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not in total. The initial people who entered the field got a briefing on what the project was about. We're dealing with people that came for two weeks, they were -- came over a period of several months, they would stay for indeterminate times, they would come in at irregular intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to cut you off, but I don't want to keep you here until next week either.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just tell me briefly, then, you don't agree with the first sentence, that there was no systematic briefings at the sites upon arrival ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He was answering that in a reasonable manner and should be allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us decide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, would you agree with Mr. McCloskey that you had not finished your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please bring it to an end and then Mr. Meek with proceed with his next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially there was systematic briefings for the majority of people at the beginning of the project, but as the project went on it became impossible to indoctrinate everybody about the project as they came in, because they come in at different times, different places et cetera. And again, the initial individuals, the initial individuals which were the bulk of them, did get a standard plan of operation where they were going to be. I don't know what that really refers to, but where they were going to be, what work was expected of them, and how we were going to go about it. Yes, and I do agree about the -- the difference of the purpose, because many people were from human rights backgrounds and thought we were there basically to identify people, and that was not our purpose or our mandate. And that all again falls under the personal identification. We passed on the personal identification to other organisations; that was not something in our mandate. Only if we had leads to specific identifications, we followed those up. And the chain of responsibility, as far as the field was myself and Jose Pablo, who was with the UN, and in my absence he was in charge. In the -- in the laboratory, as far as the forensic pathology was concerned, ostensibly Dr. Kirschner was in charge of the operation of the -- of the morgue, once it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. And frankly, I appreciate that answer, and I'm really not interested in Dr. Kirschner and what he may -- may have done or may not have. Thank you for your answer. So you agree there was no clear concept of the chain of the responsibility. Now, was that your fault or Mr. Jose Baraybar's fault, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I think -- I think you need to look further in this report, because this committee severely criticises administrative and logistical support that we had in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to those points, but my question was, and I'll just reread it to you. "So do you agree there was no clear concept of the chain of responsibility" you did agree with that. And my question was, "Was that your fault or Mr. Jose Baraybar's fault?"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the people didn't understand who was in charge, I guess it might be my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Might be?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you, as the overall team leader, had the responsibility to make sure people knew what the chain of responsibility was --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- and to do delegation. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And I thought I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apparently the committee didn't, though, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go down to paragraph 3 on that same page, sir. The finding of this committee was that "having two sites open at the same time caused severe logistic problems in transportation and equipment." It says, "Dr. Haglund often spent hours driving between the sites. That impeded his ability to routinely supervise the work being done." Do you agree with those findings, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I spent hours usually driving between sites at night. But, yes, there was -- there were problems when two sites were open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, real quickly, which two sites were open at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Ovcara and Pilica, and in my absences in Ovcara there was somebody in charge, and that was Dr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And it was only when I switched over to go to that, that I became --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Didn't you actually, sir, during this time give orders that bodies should not be exhumated in your absence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I did not give orders that bodies should not be exhumed. I gave -- I gave order that they should not be removed, but there were plenty of work to do cleaning them off. And I explained this already it was because we needed to have a -- a link between the lab and a link between the field in regards to these remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, when you were gone, and in your absence, couldn't Jose Baraybar have taken care of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In some instances he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why not in all instances, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Because he wasn't there all the time. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's not -- in some instances he did. In some instances I still felt Jose Pablo was not travelling between the morgue and the field, and I'm talking about a link between the morgue and the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, aren't you, in fact, talking chain of custody of the evidence, even the bodies and other evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And it was much more efficient to -- to do a -- a tape recording of this and get it put it on a record so that the pathologist could -- that was my impression, anyway, that was my decision, so that the pathologist could open up a body bag and say, yes, that is the body bag that is numbered and that is the body bag that is described as being numbered such and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly then, only you or Baraybar should be doing that and there were times when Baraybar would do it in your absence, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And there were times when you were both absent?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, no, no, no; one of us was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have to ask you, why was it that you stated you would not allow the bodies to be removed without you being present?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: At the Cerska grave I was present all the time. At the Nova Kasaba grave, Jose Pablo removed bodies in my absence and I was there sometimes and dictated removal. At the Pilica grave he was there for a lot of the time and he did all of that. At the Lazete grave, for the most part, I was there absent maybe for a day or so and, in my absence, I would ask that the bodies would be removed or returned. It did not retard the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let's just break this down. At the Cerska grave you were present all the time, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was present all the time during -- yes, during -- basically during the body-removal time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And at Nova Kasaba grave, Jose Pablo removed bodies while you were gone doing other things, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At the Pilica grave Jose was there a lot of the time --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He was there continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And then at the Lazete grave for the most part you were there and maybe absent for a few days, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it your testimony then it's the Lazete grave that this report is probably speaking to about slowing up or not going quickly enough and halting the work --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe it would be Lazete grave -- at Lazete grave 2A, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. 2A, 2B?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: 2A, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There was a 2B also, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And later on did you also discover there was actually a 2C, Lazete 2C, that you missed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I know -- I don't know what you're speaking of, if you're speaking of other remains from the Lazete 2 area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah, they called -- yeah, Lazete 2C?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah, I am aware of that, those are the bodies I left behind and are reflected in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Bodies you knew about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely. One -- I knew there was one protruding from the bank, but when the bank is caving in, you have to get out of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The committee again -- I'm going to ask you to go to the next page, please, for the e-court. Okay. You see under, "Recommendations."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Under number 2 that there should be a transmittal of knowledge, both up and down the chain of command frequently?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, that apparently wasn't happening when you were in charge, or they wouldn't have recommended that. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It did happen some of the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It didn't happen some of the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It just happened a few times?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm saying it was not a constant. I say that yes, that at some times those things broke down, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Also the recommendation to listen to suggestions carefully?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And was it you who wasn't listening to suggestions carefully, since you were the head man there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know who they were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Number 3, open only one grave site at a time to prevent excessive driving, animal scavenging and supply problems?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I would have suggested that myself. That was my original intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you were the one who had two grave sites open at once, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was not my choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Whose choice was it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So the Office of the Prosecutor's fault that you had to go to two grave sites at once?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The -- I'm not saying it's their fault. I'm saying that this happened to be the circumstances we happened to have had, the open grave -- two graves at once. Now, the work -- the work was paced so that it made the least impairment on the activities of either site. And -- and that's -- and that is -- and then the end point of it, that's why Jose Pablo finished the Pilica grave and I continued on to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think you have agreed that it is a problem to have two grave sites at one time open, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the staffing but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In this instance --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: But in this instance, yes, the logistics were horrible and that had to do with getting across to Brcko bridge, it had to do with people's airplane flights, all kinds of things beyond our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You knew at the time, why didn't you -- my question, sir, is why didn't you tell whoever was directing you from the Office of the Prosecutor, this isn't correct, I cannot do this, get someone else to finish one of the other sites so I only have one site open at a time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We had somebody else working at the other sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yet they needed you there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then why did you go?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Because I had somebody adequate to do another one while I was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So -- so that I understand your testimony, even though they recommended only having one grave site at a time open, you don't think that's a valid recommendation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I guess we're talking at cross purposes. Could you not, or did you ever request and couldn't you have requested that someone else be put in charge of, say, the Croatian grave site so you don't have to make those drives?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The beginning recommendation before we went into the field that only one site should be done at a time. That was my beginning recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And -- and the Office of the Prosecutor didn't go along with that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor thought that was a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But they didn't acknowledge it and they didn't abide by it, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Due to a three-week delay in the field we had to start another grave before we were done with all the graves. That was something we just had to do and we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again that wasn't your fault, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't this there is a -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can we move forward in this document three more pages. Yeah, that's -- that's good. Now, this committee in San Antonio also were in mutual agreement on management problems on the part of the supervisors, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you were not only one of the supervisors, you were the main supervisor, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In respect of the exhumations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Setting up -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We already discussed number one, lack of knowledge regarding the chain of command. Have we not? Do you agree with that, that there was a lack of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there was, but that's what this says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your opinion there wasn't?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think there was -- there was a basic knowledge of chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I had no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. So the committee is wrong about that mutual agreement that they made, there was a lack of knowledge regarding the chain of command by the supervisors. We'll go to number 2. That committee was in mutual agreement -- I'm not going to read it, you can read it. Lack of stating who the volunteer was specifically working for, and the little -- and little thought as to positioning less experienced personnel with more experienced anthropologists and pathologists. Do you agree or disagree with that finding, sir, or that ...

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These are recommendations of -- and I think they're all good recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I would just -- I agree with you that they're good recommendations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And frankly, after this committee meeting and -- in San Antonio in 1997, you were -- you didn't do any more work for the Tribunal after that, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, really? Where?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I spent a year and a half doing 1200 body -- reports on 1200 exhumations from 1996. I worked for the Tribunal until mid-1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me re -- let me rephrase my question. You didn't do any field work for them any longer, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: One has to write the report at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Since you finished the reports in 1998 that went back to 1996, you have not been re-employed by the -- this Tribunal, have you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I chose not to be, because I took another job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to go back to it, this page you're looking at, sir, those aren't recommendations, we've already gone through some recommendations. We're going to get to more recommendations. These were the committee's mutual agreement on management problems on the part of supervisors. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: What page are you on here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's on e-court.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: "There was mutual agreement," it starts out, on management problems on the part of the supervisors:" Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, much of this is a repetition of the previous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's 1 through 14. I know on the screen you can only see 12, but we'll get to them. Do you agree with number 3, that the committee -- that the management problems of the supervisors was lack of communication with a criminal investigation, with all its legal ramifications and trial preparation, and not simply an exercise in demonstrating violations of human rights. Do you agree with that, sir, or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's difficult for me -- anybody who is working for an International Criminal Tribunal knows it's going to go to court. That's what we're there for, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's hard me to conceive that those people were there and didn't know they were working for a criminal court. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Could it have been --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were also given briefing statements by PHR before they left of what they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, couldn't it have been, sir, that the reason some of those people weren't aware that -- the investigation was a criminal investigation is because you, as a main supervisor, never fully informed them? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 4. The supervisors, they agreed had a total lack of communication between supervisors and between supervisors and volunteer personnel. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If it was a total lack, we wouldn't have been able get any work done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you disagree with that. Well, let's go to 5. Dismissal of all non-substantive minor allegations of recklessness in vehicular operation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They dismissed it, yes. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What's that mean? Does that mean that the supervisor is just dismissing all minor allegations about people that other people were recklessly driving vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, no. That was -- that was an allegation that I drove fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Apparently it bothered some of the people there, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Apparently, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on number 7 regarding the management problems of the supervisor, they say there was little need of rapidity of some grave site exhumations and only one exhumation should have been performed at one time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We've just addressed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. I think you don't really agree with that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I told you that it is -- it is desirable to do one site at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How about rapidity?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think they also said that they didn't feel -- well -- rapidity, not knowing that you're not going to be there the next day, yes, I think there was -- you needed to be efficient. And if the efficiency is -- is translated into rapidity, then I think it's needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So then again, I take it you don't agree with number 7, the first part of it anyway, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not in this context, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Let's go to 8. That panel mutually agreed that there was some validity to the charge of shifting and non-protection of the bones. Do you agree with that or not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know what that is referring to, so I can't address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You were the main forensic pathologist in charge of the bones, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I just don't know what that refers to. I don't know the context and what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Number 9. The panel mutually agreed there was too much subjectivity and not enough objectivity in the performance of the exhumations and post-mortem exams. And I'm not even considering the post-mortem exams because you didn't -- weren't involved in that part of it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I just don't know what -- what some of these are referring to. But that's -- that's certainly their -- what is the heading of this, by chance? I didn't see the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The heading of whole document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, no, no. The heading of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There was mutual agreement on management problems on the part of the supervisors.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, these are very experience people. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You were the main supervisor and you don't know what they were talking about in number 8?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: You asked about bones, I just don't know -- I don't know with -- what context they're talking about. Which bones? I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is that, as I told you, promises sometimes are short lived and there has been some overlapping and the interpreters have missed some of the statements made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can't reach him from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- if you look at the current page on the transcript, you should know exactly what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thought he said something about very strange people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him say that, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall that we were talking about -- there was a mutual agreement on the management problems on the part of the supervisors, and you said okay, and then I must have said okay, and then you said something about very strange people. What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about very strange people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, what I heard was, these were very experienced people, is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And are we talking very experienced people, the members of the panel who made -- that were all in mutual agreement --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- on the supervisors -- [Realtime transcript read error, "Someone tw?"]

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They have resourced very high-tech facilities in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please, Witness, Dr. Haglund and Mr. Meek, if you have a look at the screen, you will see the problems that the interpreters are encountering. So if you could kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will try to, judge, but seriously the last time he started to answer my question before I even finished it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, Mr. Meek. I'm appealing to both of you to slow down and not to overlap. So if you could kindly repeat your question, please, Mr. Meek. Last we heard from the witness was they have resourced, very high technical facilities in the United States. And that supposedly was in reply to a question of yours which laconically shows up in the transcript as "Someone tw?" This is what I mean. If you slow down, it helps everyone to be able to follow better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think the question was the very experienced people you were discussing earlier, I asked you, do you mean the members who comprised the committee who did this report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, they were all in mutual agreement that one of the management problems on the part of the supervisors under number 9 was that there was too much subjectivity and not enough objectivity in the performance of the exhumations. Do you agree with that or not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I would agree with it. I'm not really sure in what -- what they're referring to. These are -- you know, these are big statements. And -- in some respects, probably, yes. And in some respects probably no, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Under number 10 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a query here we just want to make sure. The answer on line 7, page 66 and my apologies to you, Mr. Meek, for interrupting you like this. The answer -- first part of the witness's answer is" I would agree with it." Did you say I would agree with it or I wouldn't agree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, under number 10, they stated and were in mutual agreement that there was no attempt to schedule or coordinate anthropological and pathological investigations. Do you agree with the panel's finding on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If they -- they meant that there was no attempt to join the field process of the exhumations which was in the very high security area, with the goings on in the laboratory, which was in a low security area and there was no travel very much between, that's -- that's correct. If they mean that there was -- that -- but there was the -- there was a coordination, but there wasn't a coordination between the staff of both because of logistical problems, security concerns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Under number 11 there was mutual agreement by the committee members that there was too much concern with regard to media involvement. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. And in -- in the United States we were very, very concerned about media and very controlling of media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: But we were not in the United States, and I was asked to give press briefings regularly by the Office of the Prosecutor and I did so, and related procedurally what we did. Not any information about the actual evidence, but I did that on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in -- and, in fact --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And -- excuse me, in contrast to the United States or Canada or most of our home countries, we would not do that in a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall the colleague who made that complaint specifically to this committee that you were always in front of the camera and spending too much time in front of the camera? Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I did sleep sometimes. Yes, I was the only person that did the media at the request of the Tribunal. And many people felt that -- that I must have been you know, wanted media attention. I don't want media attention, but I was filling the wishes of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could that have been Patrick Meyers when he stated he thought the integrity of the sites was compromised by your self-promotion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no idea of what his thoughts were. At no time -- the media was kept at a perimeter, they were outside like we would have in a normal crime scene. We spoke with them away -- away from the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: With one exception. At the request of the Prosecutor, I -- the -- at the Cerska grave they wished to have -- to allow the media to photograph wires on the bound wrists of -- of a -- of a remains. And we draped off the grave and escorted the media in there to take a picture and escorted them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And while that was being done all the work had to stop, I presume?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Had to stop while people were having their lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you saying that you agree with that procedure, this -- what you just testified to?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's -- it's not something we would normally do. We're not in the United States and Canada, we're in a -- a very high internationally high-profile case, and it was something that the Prosecutor's office felt should be made public. And these graves, and that's what they wanted to do and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I guess my question is simply, did you agree with it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That particular -- that particular? No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm the supervising forensic pathologist and I don't believe it's proper and I'm not going to do it. It may affect the integrity of the site. Sir, did you tell anybody that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I am not the supervising pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And I did not feel it affected the integrity of the site. It's just something one would not normally do at a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, they made recommendations on the next page, if we could see it on e-court. And while you're looking for it, sir --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I think they're wonderful recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you have a copy of that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've read it before you came to court?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you read it after it came out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me ask this question for clarification's sake. I understand that the procedure was the witnesses were not tape-recorded and they weren't given any -- they weren't to give any written statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what I read in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what happened with you, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. After it was over do you recall when the recommendations came out? Was it fairly immediate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't recall. They don't have a release date on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. February 12th of 1998, the last page, you can look at it, you have it yourself in there.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that after February 12th you didn't discuss these findings, recommendations, with either Walter Birkby, Vincent de Majo, Richard Frody [phoen], Elis Curly, or, frankly, all of the people on the -- any or all of the people on the committee?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you discuss the findings with Peter McCloskey can I or any of the people at the Office of the Prosecutor, the OTP here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I discussed these when I testified in the proofing for the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In Krstic and for this case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't discuss it, we just went over that this was going brought up, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's what I get back to, sir, you recall earlier you said -- I asked you about the proofing session you had before Krstic and you -- I think you more or less indicated that you didn't really discuss the people, all the people who had made complaints against you just one or two young colleagues. And now I'm understanding you to say that you discussed this --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I said -- we discussed that we would be dealing with this report, and I should be aware that we're dealing with the report. As far as specifics, no, we didn't discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you read it beforehand, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that all the committee recommendations under Roman numeral VIII, 1 through 18, were not only good recommendations but came out of -- flowed from all the chaos that happened during your time in Bosnia, sir? And again the Judges are going to get mad at one of us, so while I'm asking a question, you should really listen until I finish and I will try to listen to your answers, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It's argumentative. And that's the -- creating the problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Meek. Do you wish to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't think it's argumentative. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to respond to that, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The work that Dr. Haglund has done his whole career, the work he did there, to be described to him after the summer he put in as "chaos" is an insult and is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let him respond to it. I mean, he can agree or disagree with that. Basically that's what he is here for, to answer the questions. Let me consult with my colleagues. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in agreement here that the question in itself, as put, is flawed, especially because it is attributing to the witness all the chaos that you allege to have happened or which you believe to have happened during his time in Bosnia. So we don't think that it was a proper way to -- proper question to put to the witness. However, it has been put, and I think at this point in time we should give the opportunity to the witness to answer that question, if he can answer, or if he wishes to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not chaos. We had many problems beyond our control in situations and circumstances beyond our control and, as this committee says, they felt that the work done, under the conditions it was done, was the best work that could have been done under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could we have on e-court Exhibit 2D73? It would be -- first page of that I'd like shown to the witness would be 0036 on the e-court number, I believe. There we go. Mr. Haglund, do you recall being in a seminar --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Crimes of war project?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like the witness to be shown page 0039 from that exhibit, please. There we go. Third paragraph -- the second full paragraph down, this is your statement, is it not, sir? "I slow plate this one and that's one of the reasons -- I had a four-ring circus going on. I was going absolutely crazy here. But sometimes you're lucky and you have had the resources to cover the grave and sometimes you're not." Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that was your statement in regard to these digs in 1996 in Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was a characterisation of how, in a post-conflict environment, when you're doing these things, that's how you feel. Yes. And you have to regulate the pace of -- of the work. And sometimes you, umm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you finished with your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of the "slow plate", umm, this -- yeah. Yeah, but yes, things get crazy in these situations, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you just testified under oath here that there was no chaos there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't equate things getting crazy with chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, we're both Americans, so we're pretty much -- we know what a three-ring circus or that term means, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that three-ring circus is defined in Merriam-Webster dictionary as something wild, confusing, engrossing or entertaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this is not relevant or probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have a witness here under oath telling me it wasn't chaotic at the time. I have him giving the statement that it was a four-ring circus and that -- these are absolutely two different positions. And he doesn't want any question about this -- I have a view the Prosecutor doesn't want me to because they're inconsistent statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. It's a question of style, Mr. Meek. And I suggest that you rephrase your question and you can ask the witness to explain what he meant by a "four-ring circus," without necessarily referring to the Webster, which is not necessarily the dictionary we consult on this side of the pond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well that's true, and actually, Your Honours, while you were deliberating, some of my colleagues said they never heard of a three-ring circus. Americans, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Tell the -- the Court what a three-ring circus is, first, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's when you have a circus with three events or activities going on at the same time. And this was four events going on at the same time. We all juggle many events at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, again, you would agree with me that a three-ring circus is what you just said, a circus with simultaneous performances in three rings or the at one time, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, and it doesn't necessarily mean it's chaotic. It just means that things are going on. They can be going on very regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me though that another connotation from the slang three-ring circus is that something is wild or confusing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If that's the way a person uses it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that the synonym of confusing is befuddled, bemused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek. Mr. Meek, you've both made your point here. Let's move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Frankly, while it wasn't chaotic, it was worse than a three-ring circus. Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, three-ring circuses are very entertaining and very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take my advice, Mr. Meek, and let's move to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You will agree with me, will you not, sir, that at the time this investigation and panel was empaneled in San Antonio to look into these allegations of malfeasance, so to speak, this was a million-dollar baby for the Tribunal, money invested in the case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I think you would agree with me that you also stated at that same symposium that since 1996 the international forensic investigations up on the front stage now are giant missions, they're complicated logistically, they're expensive, in the million-dollar range, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And this was one of them, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's the first time ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. And if you know, can you tell me why it was that the Office of the Prosecutor wanted to get all these professionals together down in San Antonio to go over this, all these reports, on these four grave sites, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They wanted to make sure that these -- that -- that these allegations were -- were taken an independent look at them by independent experts to see what they thought they could be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have any idea who picked these "independent experts"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that the Office of the Prosecutor put together the panel of the independent experts to whitewash the shoddy job and sloppy science that was done by you and others at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Move to your next question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour, for the record, I don't know why. I think we're supposed to put the case to the witness sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness doesn't answer for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, Mr. President. I get confused sometimes in the afternoon and morning like we all do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Quarter to 6.00. I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have got two, at least two Defence teams that would like to cross-examine this witness. One of which is the Pandurevic team; that requires 30 minutes. Madam Fauveau, you asked for 10 minutes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But in fact I won't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: My approach will be entirely flexibility. I have no wish to bring this witness back next week. If there is time at the end of the day, I will take it, if not, I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will try to speed this up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break at quarter to 6.00 anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let's just talk about your qualifications. You are a mortician, first, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes embalmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: An embalmer. You have a mortician's licence, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't keep it up anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I know that. Back when you became the medical examiner in King County Washington that's what you were doing, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was not a medical examiner, I was a chief medical investigator. The medical examiner has to be a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Isn't it a fair statement that to be a chief medical investigator, you really have to have no prior skills that can be done by a mortician or embalmer, a -- is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In my case it wasn't. Yes, the qualification to be a medical investigator in the United States are very -- on equal, in fact. I was co-author of the volume that established the criteria for certifying medical investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. But back when you became -- into that position, you could have -- an EMT or a police officer, any layperson could have gotten that position, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The -- the preference of -- of choice was either persons with police investigative background, individuals with anatomical, medical background, or people from the funeral industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Those were preferences?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Those were preferences, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My question was, you didn't have any of those to become what -- to get that job. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I had to have qualifications to -- to -- to take this job, and I can tell you what they based my qualifications on, but I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let's just go into your duties. Wouldn't it be a fair statement that you -- when you were working this job as an investigator for the King County, Washington medical examiner's office, your basic duties were to go to a crime scene, make sure the body was put into the bag, escort it to the morgue, make sure it arrived at the morgue where the pathologist took over?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. In your career can you tell the Tribunal approximately how many times that you've testified in criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In an international context this is my fifth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in the domestic setting in the United States?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Four maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Really?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think you testified earlier today that during this time you had over 2.000 cases. You worked on 2.000 cases?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The office took jurisdiction over 17 to 1500 cases a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The -- the operating procedure in our office, because of court time spent, time away from staff spent by investigators, was that the forensic pathologist would accompany us to homicide cases, because they were the most likely to appear in court, and that the forensic pathologist -- that -- the forensic pathologist would then have an oversight over the complete case from the scene through the autopsy, and they would be the only person that would testify in court. As -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And of all these times that you have testified have you ever testified on the behalf of a person accused of a crime or only on -- for the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I've only testified on behalf of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier in the day you were asked a question by my learned colleague, Mr. McCloskey, and I'll say it's on page 16, line 8 on regarding Clyde Snow. He said, Mr. McCloskey, "Can you tell us a bit about your knowledge of Clyde Snow, his reputation and your connection to him?" You answered that question, and the next question at line 19 was, "Is he one of the top people in this field?" I'm going to ask you that same -- I don't think you answered. Your answer was, "Well, he certainly is a pioneer in international human rights forensic work and the application of forensic anthropology and archaeology, especially in Latin American countries." But I would like to ask you, as Mr. McCloskey did, is he one of the top people in this field, if not the top person in this field in the world?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He's one of the top yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who, in your mind, is higher than him, sir? You?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It depends on what context you're asking this question. If you're asking it in terms of people with -- in forensic anthropology who have other -- other interests and fields that they go into, there are other people that are more expert than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just name one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We would like rate people in the U.S. but I don't see why it's necessary here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Fine, I withdraw the question. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you will agree, doctor -- or Mr. Haglund, I'm sorry, I would like to get this done with so I'm trying -- going to try to ask you yes or no questions, the best I can. Will you agree with me that it was Clyde Snow who established your work in the human rights, humanitarian rights, forensic anthropology area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It wasn't just Clyde Snow, it was also Eric Stover, who was the director of the Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember giving an article saying that you had pestered Clyde Snow -- had pestered after meeting him when he was a professor at Washington?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He was not a professor at Washington state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He came and talked there, lectured there, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have know idea whether he came and lectured there. He came to work on a case with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall making that statement ever that you had pestered Clyde Snow to get you into it -- help you get into this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: All of the forensic anthropologist pestered Clyde to go on an international mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm specifically speaking about an interview you gave as part of the institute -- I think it's the institute of human rights, conversations with history. It was a series on uses of Internet technology with the public -- Berkeley's distinction. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, Harry Chrysler, is that his name?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Interviewed you, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that's when actually you told Harry that you weren't a vicarious [sic] reader, you'd actually flunked the second grade the first time you took it. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then you told him, did you not, that, "I had known Clyde Snow for meetings and he had done some consulting in the Green river case so I pursued my degree and I kept pestering Snow about going on an international mission." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You didn't mention anybody else that you pestered besides Clyde Snow, though, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you a member of the American Board of Forensic Anthropology?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever been?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware then, do you have any knowledge of that association?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And Dr. Kathy Reich, who was the expert witness for the Defence in the Rwanda case, is a diplomat with that group?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You will agree that is the highest statue [sic] you can attain in a group, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the inner administrational positions of the group, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever applied to get into it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did they reject you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I'm board eligible. They accepted my case work, they accepted my professional standing, they accepted my experience, and they accepted my training. I just did not take the test, as has 25 per cent of the people who are members have not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you believe that in the field that you work in it's important to maintain your objectivity and the perception of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you have also made statements that you don't believe that organisations should take money from the governments because there is a perception that you either lose your objectivity --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Non-governmental human rights organisations --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: -- don't necessarily take money from governments. However, the size of projects like this, if -- if they are going to even do these projects, they do accept money from certain parts of the governments, like the diplomatic parts, not the Department of Defence or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think what you actually said, and this was an article in the Science of Human Rights, careers in forensic science, maybe June 21st of 2002 in Austin. Do you recall that? Or Jim Austin wrote it, I'm sorry. Do you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I don't offhand, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Let me show it to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Is it something I'm supposed to have written though?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, you're quoted in it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 2D75, please. And show on the e-court, please, the front page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never seen this before, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe scroll down a little more. There.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you want to look at it and see whether you've seen it or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I've already said I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You see on down right after -- right before where it says, "International exhumation," the paragraph above it says, "'By studying the site of a mass grave,' Haglund said in a recent telephone interview, 'we can tell how it was dug,'" et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did that refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, but I -- I agree with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. In that, if you will go, please, to 0047, page 0047. And while that's coming up, sir, you have given telephone interviews and TV interviews and things like that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you seriously have no recollection of talking with Jim Austin?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I -- I really -- don't really read these things that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. The question wasn't whether you had read it. Do you recall speaking with Jim Austin over the telephone about your --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not -- I -- I spoke to him, I don't recall it. You know, yeah, I spoke to him. I don't really recall the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could we scroll a little bit up? Yeah. Keep going. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On the screen studying -- making a living study the dead. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Down on the fifth line, after the parentheses, it says, "Accepting support directly from national governments would compromise the perception of independence and, consequently, their credibility."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So my question to you is, if accepting money from a national government would compromise the perception of the independence and credibility?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Don't you think that accepting money from the Office of the Prosecutor on a criminal case does the same -- has the same effect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know if the Physicians for Human Rights got any money from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, but you did, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was employed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We're talking here about NGOs accepting money, not -- not forensic experts being paid for a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We're not paid for our opinion. We're paid for our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: To get back really quickly, you know a Chester Moore, a Ph.D., a forensic anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I worked with you on some of these digs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically the time-frame in 1996 in what location?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If I consult my reports, I can tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, we are going to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before we proceed, we are, for this last session of today's sitting, sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, because Judge Kwon had to leave. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Briefly, before the break, I asked you about Chester Moore, Ph.D., a forensic anthropologist that worked under you at these sites, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that it's a fact that Chester Moore left basically in disgust because of the way things were being run on these digs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no idea of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we have on e-court 2D78. Which, while that's coming up, it is an article entitled, "All that remains: Identifying the victims of the Srebrenica massacre." From the human rights centre and human rights -- DNA and human rights. Could you please show the witness page 0059 of that document? And scroll down, please. All right. Thank you. Now, the very last paragraph, sir, and I believe Mr. Haglund, that they're quoting you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This is beginning 1998 or the PHR Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: "By 1998, many of the Srebrenica survivors began to acknowledge," okay. On down it says, the sentence, "The survivors wanted the world to acknowledge that they had been victims of genocide, and the remains provided their proof. But the ICTY's timetable for exhuming the Srebrenica graves held the unearthed remains essentially hostage to prosecutorial priorities and The Hague's logistical capacity al capacity."?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Who authored this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If we go back to the first page, Laurie Vollen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you know Laurie Vollen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I will ask you, sir, was that true?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what I asked you who authored this, because I didn't write this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, you didn't?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Let me read it -- let me read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to go back to 0059, I'm sorry. And scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there's more to this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he could comment on something, it's mid-sentence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm just asking the witness, Your Honour to read the last paragraph, if he will. And again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And sir, as soon as you've finished that page, we can flip this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Let me -- this is somebody else's words, and -- and -- and I -- I don't know why she would say some of these things. I can understand, but I don't -- I don't think it's good for me to speculate why somebody else says something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm not going ask you to do that, sir. Just read it and tell me when you've finished with it and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if we could see the next paragraph too. Which other part, Mr. McCloskey, were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to get that last sentence so we have the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Exactly. And I agree. I showed it to him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could scroll up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Up again means to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bottom of the page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you want me to look at the last sentence of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then it goes on from there, "The Hague logistical," tell me when you're finished reading that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're just asking him to read that last sentence, right, not the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, not next paragraph, just finish that sentence ending up with investigations period finishing up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You know Laurie Vollen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I've never given interviewed with her, but she was a -- an employee of PHR and we insisted that there be somewhere for the remains to go to be identified and they started that project and we handed off the remains to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.
