Now, my question to you, since you were the supervisor in this -- on these digs and exhumations, if you know, and I think you know you've been brought here as an expert, what -- what does she mean that, "But the ICT's [sic] timetable for exhuming the Srebrenica graves held the inert remains essentially hostage to prosecutorial priorities and The Hague's logistical capacity." What did she mean, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Umm, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, given the time-frame that this is talking about, 1998; he ended in 1996. It really gets speculative when we're going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He already testified he was still writing reports in 1998, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Writing reports in 1998 is one thing and answering for -- trying to explain the terms used by someone else in the context of 1998 is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Briefly, before you went into the field, were you briefed by any investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Jean-Rene's a team six investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Jean-Rene's what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Team six. I think he's already testified, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he the only one?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I accompanied the team into the field to do assessments, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And what was it that he told you as to what you were looking for and what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: What I was looking for was to make sure that there were graves there, assess tat they were graves, and assess the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Didn't -- did at any time Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez tell you that the OTP believed there to be X amount of bodies buried?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The only estimate I ever heard, and I don't know who I heard it from, was 1200 remains, maybe, at the Branjevo Farm Pilica grave site. That doesn't mean anything to me; it's how many bodies are in the grave that concerns me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand that. But do you recall ever being -- giving an interview to a newspaper where you quoted the figure of 7.000 dead or missing and presumed dead, Bosnians Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that came from the International Committee of the Red Cross as public information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And no one from the OTP ever told you that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in regards to your testimony in Krstic, sir, did you, in your capacity as the forensic anthropologist on these four digs, what weight, if anything, did you give to the fact that many of the bodies you exhumed had civilian clothing and the -- no ID cards?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a fact that I -- I reported in a report. I had no opinions on it. It's just a fact that I reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore you didn't make assumptions that all the bodies found were civilians, if they had civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: All I could -- all I could report was my observation that they had civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And to you, and I'm asking you today --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They had civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you made no assumptions or conclusions that they were, in fact, civilians and not soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: There was no way I could make a -- a -- a opinion on whether they were soldiers or whether they were civilians. They had civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware, sir, that in this case there's been quite a few witnesses testify, Bosnian Muslim witnesses, that they were, in fact, in the army and on the 11th of July when they headed to Susnjari in the column, they took off their military clothes and put on their civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, but it has nothing to do with the graves, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I want to just touch briefly on -- I want to ask you first, do you know Elizabeth Neuffer, a journalist from Boston?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And tell me when did you meet her?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I met her in 1996, probably July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, she spent time with you and your team on the digs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: She spent time with the media outside the perimeter of the digs, not with our team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you talk with her?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And have you read her book, "The Key to My Neighbour's House"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, for e-court purposes, could you please put up 2D80? Okay. That -- for the record, that is the front of the book, correct? To the best of your knowledge, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we flip to the very next page, which would be 0076. And -- right there, that's fine. Now, this is -- you've read the book, you've told us, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't recall when it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sometime after 1996, I presume?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It makes a difference when it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What difference does it make, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I just want to know, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't have the exact date of it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This is chapter 9 entitled, "Bring me his body."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, that chapter essentially deals with the summer of 1996, or July of 1996, in and around Srebrenica and the exhumations and excavations that you were doing. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Did Elizabeth Neuffer in chapter 9 of that book accurately portray what was going on with the -- your team that you were supervising?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I would have to reread it to -- to recall actually, I read this book several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: To give -- give a correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. If we go to 0089, please. Could you scoot it over a little bit, perhaps. The other way. No, scoot it over so we can -- there we go. And take it up. There. About the fourth line down she says, "Not everybody liked working for Kirschner, who could be brusque and over critical." We've got to scroll back down. All right. There it is. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say, "Not everybody liked working for Haglund, who drove everybody as hard as he drove himself." And then in the book it says, "'I need someone to be the social chairman on the love boat,' he would complain, when staff wanted time off."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't ever remember saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: But it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've read this book, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- when you give an interview or when you -- when somebody else says something, that's doesn't mean that's what you did or said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Scroll down a little bit so we can see that bottom paragraph. See where it starts, "Haglund had instructed the teams at both sites to expose bodies but not to remove them until he arrived."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, we've already talked -- spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. And, "It was an approach that annoyed many of the anthropologists on the dig, used to developing their own relationship with the grave." You agree with that, don't you sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So basically since you've read this book and this chapter which deals with you, do you recall anything at all in there that was untrue?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: There are things I disagree with, yes. I think -- again, this person is not in my mind, and didn't follow me around, but this is her perception of what she saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go, please, to -- scroll up a little bit for me, if you will. Keep going. It would be two more pages. Scroll back so I can see what page that is. 0090. Sorry. There we go. I'm looking on the right side. Scroll on down. There we go. See, Mr. Haglund, where it starts, the paragraph starts, "Some of Haglund's team members accused him of being high-handed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We've already spoken about that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And on down a little bit, "Others found him dictatorial for their tastes -- too dictatorial for their tastes"? Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, some may have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Then she goes on to say, "Haglund, exhausted, worried, frantic, obsessed with getting things done, had lost the art of polite conversation." Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just one more page, it would be 0091, I think. On the left side, that's fine. You see where it says, "I never thought." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It says," -- this is quoting you, "'I never thought I would have to do more than one site at a time,' he said some years later reflecting on that summer of 1996. 'I knew it would be horrible and it was horrible. The whole summer was beyond The Hague's vision. They didn't realise how much time it would take, there was no clear direction, and we didn't have a good sense of what we were getting into.'" Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think you have to take that in the context it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think you have to take it in the context in which it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it was said -- it was said in the context --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We are going around this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we are going around and around and around and around. But basically he's given you his answer. There is no reference that I can see in this -- in this text to which we could refer to establish the context one -- supposedly the witness is reported to have made this statement. So let's move, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thanks, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The context, is it true the context was taken from that summer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The context of this, it's years afterwards, she's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. In looking back, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what she says, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, she quotes you. Did you say that or did you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know how many times you have been quoted inaccurately, but -- yes, I mean, I've said. It's true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you scoot it over to the right so we can look at the next page real quickly. You see the paragraph starts, "On another level, the Srebrenica investigation hit a major snag," and then on down sir it says, "Fearful that Defence attorneys on the case might have been handed a powerful weapon, the Tribunal and its lawyers launched an internal inquiry." The next paragraph says, "Haglund had no sooner returned to his home in Seattle for his first vacation in more than a year when he got the news he was suspended and his work was under review." Sir, I'm asking you, is it true that you had no sooner returned home from your first vacation in more than a year that you got the news that you were suspended and your work was under review?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Being an American and as litigious we are, you've never sued this woman for liable or slander or any false statements, have you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: She died in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Have you sued her estate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, wouldn't think of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Is that because she didn't make any false statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is sickening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Mr. Meek, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, in your entire career, starting with the medical examiner's office in Seattle, Washington, through to working in international war crimes, the Tribunals, with Tribunals and on digs for humanitarian reasons, and being on a team with forensic pathologists, have you ever been involved in such a case where the Prosecutor facilitated, authorised, assisted, or otherwise influenced the ultimate report which reflected the cause and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever been on such a case where the Prosecutor would edit or had the right to edit, amend, or alter final autopsy reports, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at -- it's already been admitted into evidence, it's the exhumation volume I, it would be the Lazete 2 grave site. P616 is the Prosecution number on that. I think the witness has it in front of him. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I tried to get it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These desks are small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't anyone to get hurt. Eva. Please, can we -- leave everything. If you stay away from it, no one will get hurt. But for the time being I would suggest that no one touches the mess that we have here now for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's on the screen now, doctor.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We're going to go to page -- it will be page -- ERN 1641. Or page 71. No, actually, I want -- the ERN number is 0149-1641.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And frankly, if we can back one page, Mr. Haglund, this is under Haglund can see. Scroll down. Now, do you recall this report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, can we go to the next page, please. See five lines down from the top?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You write, "Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports was facilitated by ICTY legal advisor, Peter McCloskey." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. As it's stated in the oversight report, they had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What oversight report, first?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Talking about the San Antonio report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a minute. On page 71 of that same document, if we can go to that. Which is ERN last -- ending 1713. No. It's 0149-1713. That's page 58, we need page 71. There we go. Again, under your acknowledgements, you acknowledge that the finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing and final autopsy -- editing of final autopsy reports occurred under the direction of ICTY legal advisor, Peter McCloskey, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, he facilitated by carting these things around the world to pathologists to look at their opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at this page 71, they can blow it up so you can see it better. "Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of the final autopsy reports occurred under the direction of ICTY legal advisor --"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Direction is not a proper term. I should not use "direction." He facilitated this. He facilitated the report. He didn't -- he didn't change things or anything like that. It's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you use "direction" there, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well the direction to get the reports delivered to the pathologists so they could look at them, yes, so they could make sure that their opinion was the original opinion on the report. He directed that effort. He facilitated that effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you agree with me that in each -- each of the four reports that you drafted from this --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- these excavations, you acknowledge and thank Mr. McCloskey, who you say is a legal advisor for the ICTY for finalisation of cause and manner of death as well as editing of final autopsy reports, either under his direction or being facilitated --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: "He facilitated that and he directed the logistics in getting the reports to the pathologists who confirmed their own manner and cause of death."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, we know from your prior testimony that Dr. Kirschner was changing results of autopsies without telling people, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And let me ask you this: Were you with Peter McCloskey all the time when he was -- what you say, facilitating --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- finalisation of these things?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you weren't with Peter McCloskey when he was talking to the pathologists --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- the manner and cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And if you want me, I will show you this, but this will be on the final report dated June 15th, 1998, for Pilica, Branjevo Farm grave site? Under acknowledgements, once again, you state, "Finalisation of the cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports occurred under the direction of ICTY legal advisor, Peter McCloskey."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. The effort to see that they were properly -- cause and manner of death done by the pathologists who originally did the autopsies, he directed and facilitated that effort, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He directed them. Now, you say, in an effort to see that they were properly, the manner and cause of death was proper. What expertise does a lawyer like Peter McCloskey have in directing and editing these kind of medical documents, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He sought the opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Go ahead, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He sought the opinion of the pathologists who did the actual reports to see if they were properly done to their original opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And were you with him when he did this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And this is what you are assuming, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you are assuming it's true, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I guess it's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, I'm an English speaker too, so if we can try and observe the courtesy of waiting for the running transcript to stop, we should get done in the allotted time. Now, I've had the pleasure of reading all your reports and the annexes to them. And I've listened to the criticisms that have been made of you at San Antonio, but I don't suppose one of them was a criticism of your record-keeping. Your reports are very considerable documents indeed, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we leave aside the narrative parts of them, they include the pathology reports in relation to every body or body part examined?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Complete photographic documentation, a bibliography of reference material, a complete listing of all those who worked on the sites and in the mortuary and their qualifications, and evidence logged in relation to the recovery of exhibits from the sites. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to characterise this quite quickly, but in the body of the report you explain the task you had, the work you did, your methodology, and you summarise all, as it were, the supporting material?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And yet you still thought it was necessary to annex to the report all of the supporting material as well?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm not criticising you, I'm suggesting that is good practice, because that enables everybody to look at the body of the report, go to the supporting material, and see and check whether what you say in the body of the report is right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in the body of the report also you set out a lot of the factual information in spread sheets. And I want you to consider this: Would you consider it only professional to record in those spread sheets all relevant information that was in your possession as an anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as the first supervising anthropologist in relation to this investigation, would you have expected that these good practices of retaining and producing all the supporting material and recording in the relevant spread sheets all the relevant figures and material to continue throughout the investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Continue through what investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Investigation --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The 1996 investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I dare say in 1996 you didn't foresee the events which Mr. Meek has asked you quite a lot of questions about. But would you have expected every pathologist working under you and anybody who followed you to carry on the good practices that I suggest to you your report discloses?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was really not -- I did not supervise the pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did I use the word pathologists? If I did --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- I'm very sorry, that's the confusion. I meant anthropologists. And I wonder whether you could quickly consider the question in the light of that correction, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that the answer, you would have expected them to carry on doing what you did?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, no, not necessarily. This is the first time it was -- this is the first effort report, and nobody had ever put together a report on multiple remains like this ever before in history, except maybe the -- the -- I don't think it may have been done, if at all, especially on these kinds of graves with this kind of endeavour, and the magnitude of this endeavour. So I would consider people look at these reports and do what they thought best with -- from their judgement. We have different ways to do reports, you can get the same information in different ways. Does that respond to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. It might help, actually, if I just showed you something, and maybe then we can -- I can get a couple comments from you. It's P0622. And I'd like to look at page 59, please. And that is the right page. And could we blow it up so Mr. Haglund could see it. I mean this is the sort of thing I've got in mind. This is just a sheet from -- I think your Cerska report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that it is nothing less than good practice to, as it were, fill in on a spread sheet all the information that you have that underlies it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: What's missing from the spread sheet is the actual measurement of the particular bone from which a stature is adapted, and those are available from the raw notes of the anthropologist. This was information that was recorded and incorporated into the pathologist's final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fine. But, really, the point is where you have made an age determination that is always recorded, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. But we have to say that these ages are not these -- it's -- there exists no standard of equations for establishing answer in this population. They're just starting now to get some. We just used the best we could. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Haglund, you're cutting short this cross-examination with every answer, that's something else I don't have to deal with with you. Just one or two bodies there, or body parts, if we look at for example PLC-117BP and follow it across?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: BP presumably indicates it's a body part rather than a body?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as we go across there, under the estimate, as to stature, it's got ND, I assume that stands for not done?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Let's see. This is what -- what number again, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: 117BP. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the two dashes alongside that would indicate that, as it were, there was no information to insert into those particular brackets in the table?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It might indicate that that particular body part did not give a stature -- a bone that would relate to stature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It might indicate that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It does indicate -- it does indicate that the bone -- it does not relate to stature. If you have just a head, you can't get stature out of that, you know, to have a limb bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And keeping it simple, there is nothing to put in there, in that case, is there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we go to the far right-hand side of this particular table we'll see -- we'll need to go up to see the significance of it. You've investigated the question of whether there were -- what you believe to be ligatures there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And does X indicate that -- that there was something and a gap indicates there was not, so again --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I would need to look at legend here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't think we've got time for you to do that, so I'm going to move on. I just want to look again please at one more of the entries on that, and it's PLC-13 -- bear with me.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: PLC-125BP, we'll have.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 124BP. And there we see an age range of 15 to 19, and accepting all the difficulties you acknowledge, that's a typical sort of age range that -- that you might have picked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move on, now, please, to, briefly, the question of age determination. I'd like you to be shown on e-court, please, P0611 at page 51. Thank you very much. Just read that over to yourself, and I just want you to clarify one thing for me?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you have, tell me when you have read it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. In the table we just saw there were age ranges given in relation to each of the items examined. Given the restrictions of time, I have to ask you this: You will agree, won't you, that elsewhere in this report you gave age ranges of 11 to 15, 16 to 25, 26 to 35, et cetera, to assess, as it were the occurrence of the ages of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, where you say there that the minimum and maximum age are equal to minus one and plus one standard error respectively, is that the minimum and maximum age of the individual age range expressed, or the collective age range expressed elsewhere in the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's the individual age range -- it's a -- goes for all of the -- all of the estimates, it's plus one minus one deviation, standard deviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would that not also mean that the groupings are subject to a similar deviation, if every individual estimate is subject to such a deviation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying, that the calculations are for each individual are subject to that. That's a -- that's a -- it's a normal way to report. There is an error measurement and, actually, I go on to say that the error measurement in this population is probably could be outside of this range because we do not really have standards for this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you. We now from Mr. Baraybar who gave evidence yesterday that at this stage we're using the Suchey Brooks technique to age these -- these body parts, which was dependent upon a North American standard, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what part of -- yes, but it depends on what part we had to do the age. If all we had was just a shoulder, we would use the distal clavicle. So it's not all Suchey Brooks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So I want you, lastly, in the few minutes we have available, to look at one further document and I'd like you to answer two questions for me in relation to that. And it's P02477 at page 8. Now, I know this isn't your document and you may not have seen it. This is a summary of all the sites exhumed as part of this investigation prepared by Mr. Baraybar, but really just a couple of questions about that. Would you expect that each of the age groupings set out at the top there ought to be expressed as having a plus or minus one error factor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not necessarily. He's not putting in individual ages, he's just putting age ranges for a whole group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly this: In, as it were, good practice record keeping and spread sheet entry, where you see nothing written there, you don't -- you would expect that to reflect the fact that simply no information to input?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what I would assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Mr. Re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Haglund, your testimony finishes here. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for having come over to give testimony and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned. And have a nice weekend. I don't think we have time for the documents. I think we have to leave it until the next day. Also because I have a meeting. We have a meeting now. So let's leave everything until Tuesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
